Landscaping Kennewick: Building Yards That Survive the Shrub-Steppe

Kennewick sits in a high desert that gets seven-ish inches of rain a year, bakes past 100°F for stretches of summer, and scours everything with wind — yet drive its neighborhoods and you'll see green lawns, maples, and rose beds. The trick is imported water: the Kennewick Irrigation District's canal system delivers Yakima River water to much of the city from spring through fall, and that irrigation season defines local landscaping. Everything you plant either lives on that system, survives without it, or dies.

Landscaping in Kennewick: what to know

That reality is pushing local landscape design in two directions at once. Traditional turf-and-trees yards remain the norm and work fine on KID water — with smart irrigation design doing the heavy lifting. But xeriscaping has real momentum here: native and adapted plantings (rabbitbrush, yarrow, ornamental grasses, desert-adapted perennials) that shrug off heat, wind, and the shoulder weeks when canal water hasn't started or has already stopped. The best local designs blend both — turf where it earns its water, waterwise zones everywhere else.

From full-yard design and installation to renovation of a wind-beaten backyard, we can connect you with landscaping contractors who build for Tri-Cities conditions.

Common landscaping situations in Kennewick

Yards designed for the wrong climate

Plant lists imported from western Washington die here — moisture-loving shrubs cook against south walls, and shade-lawn mixes fry by July. The fix is designing to this climate's strengths: sun-loving perennials, drought-adapted structure plants, and wind-tolerant trees that don't snap in gust events.

Irrigation-season whiplash

KID water typically flows mid-spring through mid-fall; outside that window, landscapes are on their own or on expensive city water. Designs that ignore the shoulder seasons show it — spring die-back and October browning. Good designs weight plantings toward species that tolerate the dry margins.

Wind exposure and soil that blows

New developments on former shrub-steppe, especially up toward Southridge and the Horse Heaven ridge, take wind that desiccates plants and strips mulch. Windbreak planting, heavier mulches (rock beats bark in exposed zones), and staked young trees are local necessities, not extras.

How it works

  1. 1

    Site and water assessment

    A designer reads your lot — sun exposures, wind path, soil (sandy loess or caliche-bound), and critically, your water source: KID irrigation, city water, or both. That water answer shapes every downstream choice.

  2. 2

    Design with zones

    Expect hydrozoning: thirsty plantings grouped where irrigation is efficient, waterwise zones at edges and slopes, hardscape where nothing should be fighting the climate. Good local designs also plan for wind, not just sun.

  3. 3

    Installation in season

    Spring and fall are planting windows; summer installs need irrigation running from day one. Hardscape and irrigation go in first, plants second, mulch immediately — bare soil here blows away or bakes.

  4. 4

    Establishment care handoff

    The first two summers decide whether trees and shrubs establish. You leave with a watering schedule tuned to your system, staking checks, and a plan for the irrigation-off shoulder weeks.

What landscaping costs in Kennewick

Landscape spending in the Tri-Cities runs the full spectrum: irrigation repair and bed refreshes at the low end, full-yard design-and-install projects in the five-figure range, scaling with hardscape (patios, retaining walls, outdoor kitchens are the cost drivers, not plants). Two local economics worth knowing: xeriscape conversions cost real money upfront but cut both water bills and maintenance permanently, and new-construction yards in developing areas often need soil amendment budgeted — builder-grade lots here are frequently compacted subsoil and caliche that plants can't root in unamended.

Frequently asked questions

What plants actually thrive in Kennewick?

The winners share a profile: sun-loving, drought-tolerant once established, wind-flexible. Locals lean on ornamental grasses, yarrow, lavender, rabbitbrush, sedums, catmint, and adapted trees like honeylocust and desert willow. Anything labeled 'moist, rich soil, part shade' is a west-side plant that will struggle here.

When does irrigation water run in Kennewick?

KID's delivery season generally runs from spring startup (around April) to fall shutdown (mid-to-late October), varying by year and canal maintenance. Landscapes need a plan for the dry margins — established waterwise plants handle it; new plantings and thirsty turf need supplemental water those weeks.

Is xeriscaping ugly? I don't want a gravel yard.

The gravel-moonscape reputation is outdated — modern xeriscape design is layered, colorful, and seasonal, built from flowering perennials, grasses, and structural shrubs. The Tri-Cities has strong examples in newer public plantings. 'Right plant, right place' is the principle; rock mulch is just one tool.

How much does a full backyard landscape cost here?

Design-and-install for a typical suburban backyard spans widely based on hardscape share — planting-focused renovations sit at the lower end, while patio-wall-kitchen projects multiply the budget. Phasing is normal and smart: irrigation and hardscape first, plantings in the following season's budget.

Do landscapers here handle irrigation systems too?

The established ones do — irrigation design is inseparable from landscape design in this climate, and most full-service outfits install and service systems including KID hookups, filtration (canal water carries sediment), and smart controllers that actually fit local evapotranspiration rates.
